fuentes/carta-de-pero-vaz-de-caminha/tit.texto: Letter of Pero Vaz de Caminha

fuentes/carta-de-pero-vaz-de-caminha/res.texto: Letter to King Manuel I dated May 1, 1500, from the “Land of Vera Cruz,” which recounts day by day the arrival of Cabral's fleet, the first encounters with the Tupiniquim (their nakedness, their adornments, the exchange of objects) and the Mass of April 26. It describes the Indians as an innocent people, easy to convert, notes that he saw no metals, and reports that it was decided to leave two degredados there so that they could learn the language.

fuentes/carta-de-pero-vaz-de-caminha/por.texto: It is the first written description of Brazil and its peoples; kept in the Torre do Tombo, it was not published until 1817.

fuentes/regimento-de-tome-de-sousa/resum.texto: Instructions from John III, dated December 17, 1548, to the first governor-general: to build a fortress and a city in Bahia, to punish the Tupinambá who had destroyed the captaincy, to favor the allied and converted Indians, to prohibit raids on Indians at peace, and to organize justice, the treasury and defense.

fuentes/regimento-de-tome-de-sousa/por_q.texto: It is the founding document of the general government and, like all later Portuguese policy, it combines war against hostile peoples with the protection of allies.

fuentes/regimento-de-tome-de-sousa/leer..texto: Document 3 of «Documentos de legislação indigenista colonial, Parte 1 (1500-1700)», CEstA, Universidade de São Paulo (PDF)

fuentes/cartas-de-nobrega/resumen.texto: Letters from Nóbrega to his superiors, to the King and to other Jesuits about the mission: cannibalism, the aldeias, the resistance of settlers and Indians, epidemics and illegal enslavement. In the one of 1558 he proposes “subjecting” the Indians by force, forbidding them to eat human flesh and waging war without the governor's license, and gathering them into aldeias with a judge and a missionary.

fuentes/cartas-de-nobrega/por_que_import.texto: They document the Jesuit program in Brazil and its ambivalence: defense of the Indians' freedom against the settlers, and use of force for conversion.

fuentes/cartas-de-nobrega/leer.0.titulo.texto: 1886 edition, «Cartas do padre Manoel da Nobrega» (Internet Archive)

fuentes/dialogo-de-la-conversion-del-gen.texto: Dialogue on the Conversion of the Gentile

Dialogue between two Jesuits, the blacksmith Mateus Nogueira and the interpreter Gonçalo Álvares, on whether the Indians of Brazil can be converted. It concludes that they have a soul and understanding like any people, and that the difficulty comes from their customs and their lack of subjection, not from their nature.
It is the first theological text written in Brazil and sets out the Jesuit position against those who denied the Indians' capacity.
Edition by Sálvio M. Soares (2006), MetaLibri, PDF on ibiblio

fuentes/cartas-de-anchieta/titulo.texto: Letters, Information and Historical Fragments of José de Anchieta

fuentes/cartas-de-anchieta/resumen.texto: Letters and reports by Anchieta: the founding of Piratininga, the war of the Tamoios and the truce of Iperoig, the epidemics of 1562–1563 in Bahia and the hunger that followed, when many Indians sold themselves or their children into slavery, and the Informação do Brasil e de suas capitanias (1584), with an account of the aldeias.

fuentes/cartas-de-anchieta/por_que_impor.texto: They are the most continuous Jesuit testimony on the second half of the 16th century and on the decline of the coastal Tupi population.

fuentes/de-gestis-mendi-de-saa/titulo.texto: The Deeds of Mem de Sá

fuentes/de-gestis-mendi-de-saa/resumen.texto: Latin epic poem, printed without an author's name in Coimbra (1563) and attributed to Anchieta, which celebrates the campaigns of Governor Mem de Sá against the Tupinambá of Bahia, the Caeté and the French of Guanabara. It narrates with approval the burning of villages and the killing of enemies as a holy war that paves the way for conversion.

fuentes/de-gestis-mendi-de-saa/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the first printed epic poems about America and shows how the Jesuits justified war against peoples who did not accept subjection.

fuentes/arte-de-gramatica-anchieta/titul.texto: Art of Grammar of the Language Most Used on the Coast of Brazil

fuentes/arte-de-gramatica-anchieta/resum.texto: Grammar of the coastal Tupi, written by Anchieta from the 1550s and used in manuscript copies before being printed in Coimbra in 1595. It describes the pronunciation, morphology and regional variants of the language that the Jesuits used in catechesis, theater and confession.

fuentes/arte-de-gramatica-anchieta/por_q.texto: It is the first grammar of a language of Brazil and the basis of the “língua geral” that was spoken in São Paulo and Amazonia until the 18th century.

fuentes/singularitez-thevet/resumen.texto: Account of the voyage and stay in Guanabara Bay, with descriptions and engravings of the Tupinambá, their war, religion and cannibalism, of animals and plants, and one of the first European descriptions of tobacco, the “petun.” It mixes his own observation, reports from Norman interpreters and classical learning.

fuentes/singularitez-thevet/por_que_impo.texto: It was the first French book on Brazil and one of Montaigne's readings for his essay on cannibals; Léry attacked it for errors and inventions.

fuentes/warhaftige-historia-staden/titul.texto: True History and Description of a Country of Naked, Fierce Man-Eating Savages

fuentes/warhaftige-historia-staden/resum.texto: Account of Staden's two voyages to Brazil and of his nine months as a prisoner of the Tupinambá, followed by a description of their life, their war and the ritual in which they killed and ate their captives. It carries a preface by the physician Johann Dryander, who vouches for its truthfulness, and woodcuts made according to the author's instructions.

fuentes/warhaftige-historia-staden/por_q.texto: It is one of the most cited direct testimonies on Tupinambá cannibalism and agrees in essentials with Léry, Thevet and the Jesuits; it was written for a Protestant public, in a key of providential salvation. Its engravings, redrawn by De Bry (1592), fixed the European image of the American cannibal.

fuentes/histoire-d-un-voyage-lery/titulo.texto: History of a Voyage to the Land of Brazil

fuentes/histoire-d-un-voyage-lery/resume.texto: Account of the voyage of the Calvinists to Antarctic France (1556–1558), of the conflict with Villegaignon and of the months Léry spent among the Tupinambá: their food, their war, their religion, their songs (with musical transcription) and a dialogue in Tupi. It describes in detail the death and ritual consumption of prisoners and compares it with the atrocities of the wars of religion in France.

fuentes/histoire-d-un-voyage-lery/por_qu.texto: It is the richest 16th-century ethnography of an American people; Lévi-Strauss called it “the ethnologist's breviary.”

fuentes/historia-da-provincia-santa-cruz.texto: History of the Province of Santa Cruz

The first printed history of Brazil: it describes the captaincies, the fertility of the land, plants and animals, and the Indians, of whom it says they have “no faith, no law, and no king”; it includes Mem de Sá's wars. It was written to encourage poor Portuguese to emigrate, and it notes that the first thing settlers seek are Indian slaves for their estates.
It is an early testimony to the colonial view of the land and to the role of Indigenous slavery in the first settlements.

fuentes/tratados-de-la-tierra-y-gente-de.texto: Treatises on the Land and People of Brazil

Three texts: on the climate and nature, on the origin and customs of the Indians, and an epistolary narrative of the Jesuit visit of 1583–1590 to Bahia, Pernambuco, Rio and São Vicente, with the villages, colleges and wealth of the sugar mills. A manuscript stolen by English privateers (1601) appeared in English, without the author's name, in Samuel Purchas's collection (1625); the complete Portuguese edition dates from 1925.
It is one of the most complete descriptions of the Tupi and of the colony around 1585, written by someone who visited all the missions.

fuentes/tratado-descritivo-soares-de-sou.texto: Description of the coast captaincy by captaincy and, in the second part, of Bahia: sugar mills, plants, animals and the Indigenous peoples (Tupinambá, Tupiniquim, Aimoré and others), with their wars, their cannibalism and their kinship. It circulated in handwritten copies until Varnhagen identified the author and published it (1851).
It is the most complete description of 16th-century Brazil written by a settler, with data on the sugar economy and Indigenous slavery.

fuentes/dialogos-das-grandezas-do-brasil.texto: Dialogues on the Greatness of Brazil

Six dialogues between a veteran settler, Brandônio, and a newcomer, Alviano, on the riches of Brazil: sugar, brazilwood, cotton, cattle, plants and enslaved African labor. They are attributed to Ambrósio Fernandes Brandão, a New Christian and sugar mill owner in Paraíba.
It argues for Brazil as a settler colony and documents the sugar economy of the early 17th century.

fuentes/historia-do-brasil-vicente/resum.texto: History of Brazil from 1500 to 1627, with accounts of the wars with the Indians, the conquest of Paraíba and Sergipe, and the Dutch capture of Salvador (1624), which the author lived through as a prisoner. He criticizes the Portuguese who stay on the coast “scratching at it like crabs” and exploit the land without settling it.

fuentes/historia-do-brasil-vicente/por_q.texto: It is the first history of Brazil written by someone born in the colony; it remained unpublished until Capistrano de Abreu's edition (1888–1889).

fuentes/histoire-de-la-mission-abbeville.texto: History of the Mission of the Capuchin Fathers on the Island of Maranhão

Account of the founding of Equinoctial France (1612) and of the Tupinambá of Maranhão Island: their villages, language, religion, speeches in assembly and alliance with the French. It includes the journey to Paris of six Tupinambá and their baptism (1613), with engravings of them.
It is the main source on the northern Tupinambá before the Portuguese conquest of Maranhão.

fuentes/rerum-per-octennium/titulo.texto: History of Eight Years in Brazil

fuentes/rerum-per-octennium/soporte.texto: Printed book with maps and engravings

fuentes/rerum-per-octennium/resumen.texto: Official chronicle of Nassau's government in Dutch Brazil, written from his papers: the campaigns against the Luso-Brazilians, the capture of Elmina and Luanda, the administration of Recife, the sugar mills and the Indigenous peoples allied with the Dutch. It includes maps and engravings after drawings by Frans Post.

fuentes/rerum-per-octennium/por_que_impo.texto: It is the main source on Dutch Brazil, although it was written to glorify Nassau.

fuentes/historia-naturalis-brasiliae/res.texto: Work in two parts edited by Johannes de Laet: the medicine of Brazil by Willem Piso (diseases, poisons and remedies, many taken from the Indians), and the natural history of Georg Marcgrave (plants, fish, birds, mammals and information on the peoples and the Tupi language), with hundreds of engravings.

fuentes/historia-naturalis-brasiliae/por.texto: It was the first scientific work on the nature of Brazil and a reference for naturalists until Linnaeus.

fuentes/sermao-xiv-do-rosario/resumen.texto: Sermon preached in Bahia to a brotherhood of African enslaved people on a sugar mill. It compares the work of the enslaved at the mill with Christ's Passion and promises them salvation through patience, while describing the mill as a “hell” and reproaching the cruelty of the masters.

fuentes/sermao-xiv-do-rosario/por_que_im.texto: It shows that Vieira, an opponent of the enslavement of Indians, accepted African slavery as a means of Christianization.

fuentes/sermao-primeira-dominga-1653/tit.texto: Sermon for the First Sunday of Lent (1653)

fuentes/sermao-primeira-dominga-1653/res.texto: Preached in São Luís in March 1653 before the settlers of Maranhão, who lived off the labor of enslaved Indians captured in “rescues” and expeditions into the interior. Vieira tells them that whoever holds Indians captive unjustly is in sin and risks his soul, and proposes examining each captivity and freeing those wrongly enslaved, who could go on serving in exchange for wages.

fuentes/sermao-primeira-dominga-1653/por.texto: It is the centerpiece of Vieira's campaign against the enslavement of Indians in Amazonia, which led to the law of 1655 and, through the settlers' reaction, to the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1661.

fuentes/sermao-de-santo-antonio-1654/tit.texto: Sermon of Saint Anthony to the Fish

fuentes/sermao-de-santo-antonio-1654/res.texto: Preached in São Luís on June 13, 1654, days before Vieira traveled to Lisbon to ask for laws against the abuses of the settlers. It imitates Saint Anthony's sermon to the fish and, in allegory, reproaches the big fish for eating the small ones: the settlers who enslave Indians.

fuentes/sermao-de-santo-antonio-1654/por.texto: It is a classic of Portuguese prose and a plea against the enslavement of Indians.

fuentes/lei-de-1570/titulo.texto: Law on the Freedom of the Gentiles of Brazil (1570)

fuentes/lei-de-1570/resumen.texto: Law of King Sebastian of March 20, 1570: it prohibits the capture of the Indians of Brazil, except those taken in a just war waged with the license of the king or the governor, and those who attack Portuguese or other Indians in order to eat them, and it orders that legitimate captivities be registered.

fuentes/lei-de-1570/por_que_importa.texto: It is the first general Portuguese law on the freedom of the Indians; its exceptions, expanded or restricted by later laws, allowed enslavement for almost two centuries.

fuentes/lei-de-1570/leer.0.titulo.texto: Document 19 of «Documentos de legislação indigenista colonial, Parte 1 (1500-1700)», CEstA, Universidade de São Paulo (PDF)

fuentes/relacao-das-guerras-palmares/tit.texto: Account of the Wars Waged against the Palmares of Pernambuco (1675–1678)

fuentes/relacao-das-guerras-palmares/res.texto: Anonymous account of Governor Pedro de Almeida's expeditions against Palmares, written to his glory. It describes the mocambos and their organization, the “king” Ganga Zumba and his relatives, the royal fence of Macaco, the fortifications and crops, and the peace of 1678; it was published in the journal of the Brazilian Historical and Geographical Institute (1859).

fuentes/relacao-das-guerras-palmares/por.texto: It is the main source on the internal organization of Palmares, seen from its enemies; its population figures cannot be verified.

fuentes/constituicoes-primeiras-da-bahia.texto: First Constitutions of the Archdiocese of Bahia

Ecclesiastical laws approved at the 1707 synod convened by Archbishop Sebastião Monteiro da Vide and printed in Lisbon in 1719. They regulate the sacraments, catechesis and the life of the clergy, and order masters to let their slaves marry without separating them through sale, to teach them the doctrine, and not to make them work on holy days of obligation.
They governed the Church in Brazil until the 19th century and show what the Church demanded of masters, which was often not carried out.
First edition (Lisbon, 1719), John Carter Brown Library, Internet Archive

fuentes/cultura-e-opulencia/titulo.texto: Culture and Opulence of Brazil by Its Drugs and Mines

fuentes/cultura-e-opulencia/resumen.texto: Four-part treatise on sugar (with the running of a mill and the treatment of enslaved people), tobacco, gold mines and cattle raising, with prices and production figures. It advises masters to give enslaved people food, rest and moderate punishment, and records the saying that Brazil is “hell for Blacks, purgatory for whites and paradise for mulattos.”

fuentes/cultura-e-opulencia/por_que_impo.texto: It is the best source on the colonial Brazilian economy at the beginning of the 18th century; the Crown ordered the edition recalled shortly after printing, apparently so as not to publicize the wealth and the routes to the mines.

fuentes/nuevo-descubrimiento-acuna/titul.texto: New Discovery of the Great River of the Amazons

fuentes/nuevo-descubrimiento-acuna/resum.texto: Report of the voyage from Quito to Belém with Pedro Teixeira (1639): the course of the river and its tributaries, more than a hundred and fifty nations, the densely populated banks of the Omaguas and other peoples, their manioc and maize crops, the raising of turtles in pens, and their wars. He recommends that the King occupy the river before the Dutch do.

fuentes/nuevo-descubrimiento-acuna/por_q.texto: Together with Carvajal's, it is the main description of Amazonia before its great population collapse. After the separation from Portugal (1640), the Spanish Crown ordered the edition recalled so that it would not serve the Portuguese.

fuentes/relacion-de-carvajal/titulo.texto: Account of the New Discovery of the Famous Great River of the Amazons

fuentes/relacion-de-carvajal/resumen.texto: Account of the descent of the Napo and the Amazon (from late 1541 to August 1542): it describes densely populated banks, with villages several leagues long, roads, food stores and fine pottery, lords such as Aparia and Machiparo, and almost daily combat. It affirms that the Spanish fought with female warriors, the “Amazons,” and records from a prisoner accounts of a kingdom of women.

fuentes/relacion-de-carvajal/por_que_imp.texto: It is the first European account of the Amazon; for centuries it was considered exaggerated, and archaeology in recent decades has lent credence to its description of dense populations, though not to the Amazons. It was published in full only in 1894.

fuentes/relacion-de-carvajal/leer.0.titu.texto: Edition by J. T. Medina (Seville, 1894) with other documents on Orellana (Internet Archive)

fuentes/relation-abregee-la-condamine/ti.texto: Brief Account of a Journey through the Interior of South America

fuentes/relation-abregee-la-condamine/re.texto: Read to the Paris Academy of Sciences in 1745: the map of the course of the Amazon with astronomical observations, the description of rubber and curare, the Portuguese and Spanish missions, and a discussion of the legend of the Amazons, which the author considers possible.

fuentes/relation-abregee-la-condamine/po.texto: It was the first scientific exploration of the Amazon and it spread knowledge of rubber and curare in Europe.

fuentes/leis-de-liberdade-1755/titulo.texto: Laws of Freedom for the Indians of Grão-Pará and Maranhão (1755)

fuentes/leis-de-liberdade-1755/resumen.texto: Law of June 6, 1755 restoring to the Indians of the State of Grão-Pará and Maranhão the freedom of their persons, property and trade, annulling captivities and prohibiting any new enslavement; another of June 7 removed from the missionaries the temporal government of the villages, and a royal decree (alvará) of April of the same year had favored marriages between Portuguese men and Indian women.

fuentes/leis-de-liberdade-1755/por_que_i.texto: It legally ended Indigenous slavery in Amazonia; in 1758 it was extended to all of Brazil, although compulsory labor continued under the Directorate and enslavement reappeared with the war of 1808.

fuentes/leis-de-liberdade-1755/leer.0.ti.texto: Lisbon printing of 1755 of the law of 6 June, National Library of Portugal

fuentes/diretorio-dos-indios/titulo.texto: Directory to Be Observed in the Indian Settlements of Pará and Maranhão

fuentes/diretorio-dos-indios/resumen.texto: Regulation of 95 articles issued in 1757 by Governor Mendonça Furtado and confirmed by the King in 1758: it turns the missionary villages into towns with Portuguese names governed by a lay director, prohibits the general language and imposes Portuguese, encourages mixed marriages and European clothing, and regulates Indian labor in the crops and in service to the settlers, with a sixth of the production going to the director.

fuentes/diretorio-dos-indios/por_que_imp.texto: It was Pombal's Indigenous policy: “civilize” through assimilation. Reports of the time denounced abuses by the directors and flight, and it was abolished in 1798.

fuentes/carta-regia-de-1808-contra-los-b.texto: Royal Letter of May 13, 1808, on the Botocudos

Order from Prince Regent John to the governor of Minas Gerais declaring war on the Botocudos of the Doce River valley, accused of killing settlers and of cannibalism: it creates military divisions and authorizes keeping prisoners as captives for ten years, or while their “ferocity” lasts. Another royal letter of November 1808 extended the war to the Kaingang of the Guarapuava fields.
It de facto restored the enslavement of Indians through just war, abolished since 1755; the law of October 27, 1831 repealed it.
Coleção das leis do Brasil of 1808 (Wikisource): royal letter of 13 May, p. 37

fuentes/apontamentos-jose-bonifacio/titu.texto: Notes on the Civilization of the Wild Indians of the Empire of Brazil

fuentes/apontamentos-jose-bonifacio/auto.texto: José Bonifácio de Andrada e Silva

fuentes/apontamentos-jose-bonifacio/resu.texto: Proposal presented to the 1823 Constituent Assembly: to attract unsubdued Indians through justice and good treatment, by means of missions, trade, gifts, mixed marriages and villages under guardianship, instead of the war authorized in 1808.

fuentes/apontamentos-jose-bonifacio/por_.texto: It is the first Indigenist program of independent Brazil; it was never approved because the emperor dissolved the Assembly.

fuentes/representacao-sobre-a-escravatur.texto: Representation to the Constituent Assembly on Slavery
José Bonifácio de Andrada e Silva

Proposes ending the African slave trade within a few years and abolishing slavery gradually, with measures such as the slave's right to buy his freedom and protection for slave families; it argues that slavery corrupts masters and the nation. Written in 1823, it was published in Paris in 1825.
It is the first abolitionist plan by a Brazilian statesman; slavery lasted in Brazil until 1888.

fuentes/historia-geral-do-brasil-varnhag.texto: First general history of Brazil based on documents from Portuguese, Spanish and Brazilian archives, from the discovery to independence. It presents colonization as a civilizing work of the Portuguese and the Indians as peoples without history who had to be subdued.
It was the official history of the Empire and the documentary basis of later historiography, which debated its view of the Indians.
1854 edition, Rio de Janeiro (Internet Archive), first scan

fuentes/capitulos-de-historia-colonial/r.texto: Synthesis of colonial history that gives more room to the Indians, to the occupation of the interior by cattle and the bandeiras, to the roads and to the formation of a society of its own, than to acts of government.

fuentes/capitulos-de-historia-colonial/p.texto: It renewed Brazilian historiography and remains a standard synthesis.

fuentes/la-religion-des-tupinamba/resume.texto: Systematizes what the 16th- and 17th-century chronicles say about Tupi religion: culture heroes, shamans and prophets (karaí), migrations in search of a land without evil, and the cannibal ritual. He had studied the westward migrations, such as that of the Tupinambá who reached Peru in 1549, using Spanish documents in “Les migrations historiques des Tupi-Guarani” (1927).

fuentes/la-religion-des-tupinamba/por_qu.texto: It is the classic work on Tupinambá religion and the basis for later studies of Tupi-Guarani prophetism.

fuentes/casa-grande-e-senzala/resumen.texto: Essay on the formation of patriarchal society in the sugar-growing Northeast: it describes the master's house and the slaves' senzala as a world of intimacy and miscegenation among Portuguese men, Indian women and African women, and attributes to the Portuguese a plasticity that favored mixing. Its critics (Florestan Fernandes, Boxer and the historiography of slavery) pointed out that it softens the violence of slavery and fed the myth of “racial democracy.”

fuentes/casa-grande-e-senzala/por_que_im.texto: It is the most influential book on Brazilian identity and the fullest expression of a benign reading of Portuguese colonization.

fuentes/a-funcao-social-da-guerra/titulo.texto: The Social Function of War in Tupinambá Society

fuentes/a-funcao-social-da-guerra/resume.texto: Reconstructs Tupinambá warfare from 16th-century chronicles: it sought not land or tribute but captives, to avenge the group's own dead, and the sacrifice and ritual consumption of those captives renewed the bond with the ancestors and gave prestige and new names to the warriors.

fuentes/a-funcao-social-da-guerra/por_qu.texto: It is the classic analysis of Tupinambá war and cannibalism as a social institution, based on a critical reading of Staden, Léry, Thevet, Cardim and the Jesuits.

fuentes/the-dutch-in-brazil/resumen.texto: History of Dutch Brazil using Dutch and Portuguese sources: the Dutch West India Company, Nassau's government, the sugar economy and the slave trade, the alliances with Indians, and the insurrection that expelled the Dutch.

fuentes/the-dutch-in-brazil/por_que_impo.texto: It remains the standard synthesis in English of the period.

fuentes/golden-age-of-brazil/resumen.texto: Social history of Brazil during the gold boom of Minas Gerais: the gold rush, the War of the Emboabas, slaves in the mines, brotherhoods, smuggling, and the relationship with Portugal and England.

fuentes/golden-age-of-brazil/por_que_imp.texto: It is the standard work on the golden century.

fuentes/amazonia-counterfeit-paradise/ti.texto: Amazonia: Man and Culture in a Counterfeit Paradise

fuentes/amazonia-counterfeit-paradise/re.texto: Argues that the poverty of upland soils limited population and social complexity in Amazonia, that present-day peoples are a model of the ancient ones, and that more elaborate cultures, such as Marajoara, came from outside and declined.

fuentes/amazonia-counterfeit-paradise/po.texto: It was the dominant thesis for decades on ancient Amazonia and the target of archaeology that revealed large societies and transformed landscapes.

fuentes/red-gold/titulo.texto: Red Gold: The Conquest of the Indians of Brazil

fuentes/red-gold/resumen.texto: Narrative history of relations between Portuguese and Indians from 1500 to the expulsion of the Jesuits, based on chronicles, Jesuit letters and administrative documents: wars, alliances, villages, epidemics, enslavement and laws. It estimates the Indigenous population of present-day Brazil in 1500 at about 2.4 million.

fuentes/red-gold/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most complete synthesis of the subject in English; it is continued by Amazon Frontier (1987) and Die If You Must (2003).

fuentes/sugar-plantations-schwartz/titul.texto: Sugar Plantations in the Formation of Brazilian Society: Bahia, 1550–1835

fuentes/sugar-plantations-schwartz/resum.texto: Using the accounts of the Sergipe do Conde sugar mill, the Jesuit records and other Bahian archives, it reconstructs the shift from Indigenous to African labor between 1570 and 1620, the epidemics that accelerated it, the rhythm of the harvest, demography, and the resistance of the enslaved and the society of masters and farmers.

fuentes/sugar-plantations-schwartz/por_q.texto: It is the standard work on the sugar economy and slavery in colonial Brazil.

fuentes/moundbuilders-of-the-amazon/resu.texto: Study of the Marajoara mounds of Teso dos Bichos using geophysics and excavation: it shows mounds inhabited for centuries by large populations living from fishing and agriculture, and proposes that Marajoara was a complex chiefdom that arose locally, against Meggers's thesis of a culture that came from outside and declined.

fuentes/moundbuilders-of-the-amazon/por_.texto: It opened the archaeological revision of ancient Amazonia.

fuentes/the-pristine-myth/titulo.texto: The Pristine Myth: The Landscape of the Americas in 1492

fuentes/the-pristine-myth/soporte.texto: Article in Annals of the Association of American Geographers

fuentes/the-pristine-myth/resumen.texto: Argues that the image of a virgin America in 1492 is a myth: Indigenous peoples had transformed forests, grasslands and soils with fire, crops and earthworks, and the “wilderness” that later Europeans saw was partly the result of demographic collapse.

fuentes/the-pristine-myth/por_que_import.texto: It is one of the texts most influential in the revision of Amazonia and of all of America as humanized landscapes.

fuentes/historia-do-brasil-fausto/resume.texto: University textbook covering the history of Brazil from the colony to the late 20th century: colonization and its peoples, the sugar and mining economies, slavery, independence, the Empire and the Republic.

fuentes/historia-do-brasil-fausto/por_qu.texto: It is the standard synthesis used in Brazilian higher education.

fuentes/negros-da-terra/titulo.texto: Negros da Terra: Indians and Bandeirantes in the Origins of São Paulo

fuentes/negros-da-terra/resumen.texto: Using seventeenth-century São Paulo wills and inventories, it shows that the bandeiras were above all expeditions to capture Indians, Guaraní first, and that these captives, called “negros da terra” or “administrados” to evade the freedom laws, were the labor force of São Paulo agriculture.

fuentes/negros-da-terra/por_que_importa.texto: It replaced the heroic image of the bandeirantes as discoverers with that of a slave economy based on Indians.

fuentes/a-heresia-dos-indios/titulo.texto: The Heresy of the Indians: Catholicism and Rebellion in Colonial Brazil

fuentes/a-heresia-dos-indios/resumen.texto: Studies the “holiness of Jaguaripe,” a Tupi religious movement of the 1580s in Bahia, through the Inquisition visitation records of 1591–1592: its prophet, its rites that mixed Tupi and Catholic elements, and the protection given to it by a sugar mill owner.

fuentes/a-heresia-dos-indios/por_que_imp.texto: It is the standard work on Indigenous religious movements in colonial Brazil.

fuentes/heckenberger-2003-amazonia-1492/.texto: Amazonia 1492: Pristine Forest or Cultural Parkland?

Presents excavations in the upper Xingu carried out with the Kuikuro: large villages of their ancestors between c. 1250 and 1650, surrounded by ditches and palisades, with plazas, straight roads, bridges and intense management of the forest and wetlands. It concludes that the forest of the region is partly a built landscape.
It is one of the central pieces of evidence against the idea of an untouched Amazonia before 1492.

fuentes/heckenberger-2008-urbanismo/titu.texto: Pre-Columbian Urbanism, Anthropogenic Landscapes, and the Future of the Amazon

fuentes/heckenberger-2008-urbanismo/resu.texto: Describes two clusters of villages in the upper Xingu, connected by roads and planned around plazas, as a low-density network urbanism, distinct from compact cities, and proposes using that knowledge in present-day conservation.

fuentes/heckenberger-2008-urbanismo/por_.texto: It introduced the idea of a low-density Amazonian “urbanism.”

fuentes/parssinen-2009-geoglifos/titulo.texto: Pre-Columbian geometric earthworks in the upper Purus

fuentes/parssinen-2009-geoglifos/autor.texto: Martti Pärssinen, Denise Schaan and Alceu Ranzi

fuentes/parssinen-2009-geoglifos/resumen.texto: Describes more than two hundred geometric enclosures of ditches, circles and squares linked by roads, which deforestation exposed in Acre and neighboring areas. Interprets them as works of a complex regional society and proposes that most of them had ceremonial functions.

fuentes/parssinen-2009-geoglifos/por_que.texto: It is the reference study on the geoglyphs of Acre.

fuentes/clement-2015-domesticacion/titul.texto: The domestication of the Amazon before the European conquest

fuentes/clement-2015-domesticacion/sopor.texto: Article in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, vol. 282

fuentes/clement-2015-domesticacion/resum.texto: A synthesis of archaeology, botany and soil science: Amazonian peoples domesticated plants such as manioc, created fertile soils (terra preta), and managed forests and landscapes, with large riverbank populations that collapsed after the European arrival.

fuentes/clement-2015-domesticacion/por_q.texto: Summarizes the current consensus on the Amazon as a domesticated landscape, with its uncertainties.

fuentes/clement-2015-domesticacion/leer..texto: Open-access article (Proceedings of the Royal Society B, via PubMed Central)

fuentes/levis-2017-domesticacion/titulo.texto: Persistent effects of pre-Columbian plant domestication on the composition of Amazonian forests

fuentes/levis-2017-domesticacion/resumen.texto: Cross-references forest inventories from across the basin with the location of archaeological sites and finds that domesticated species, such as the Brazil nut, cacao or açaí, are more abundant near the sites. Crystal McMichael and others questioned its scope (in a 2017 comment, supported by their 2012 soil cores): according to them, much of the forest far from the rivers saw little human intervention.

fuentes/levis-2017-domesticacion/por_que.texto: Illustrates the current debate over how much pre-Columbian peoples modified the forest.

fuentes/prumers-2022-casarabe/titulo.texto: LiDAR reveals low-density pre-Columbian urbanism in Bolivian Amazonia

fuentes/prumers-2022-casarabe/resumen.texto: LiDAR survey of Casarabe culture settlements in the Llanos de Mojos: centers such as Cotoca and Landívar, with platforms, earthen pyramids, enclosures and causeways several kilometers long, canals and dams, occupied between c. 500 and 1400.

fuentes/prumers-2022-casarabe/por_que_im.texto: It is the first clear demonstration of low-density urban settlements in pre-Columbian Amazonia.

fuentes/historia-do-futuro/resumen.texto: «Anteprimero» book of a work that was left unfinished, in which Vieira takes up the millenarian myth of the Fifth Empire: a Christian, Portuguese empire that would succeed the four of antiquity (Assyrian, Persian, Greek and Roman) and give Portugal leadership of the world. According to Roberto de Sousa Causo it is the first utopian narrative written in Portuguese. Its composition is dated from 1649 according to Sorel or to around 1665 according to Bosi, and it was published in Lisbon in 1718, after the author's death.

fuentes/historia-do-futuro/por_que_impor.texto: It is the work in which Vieira develops the messianism of the Fifth Empire, which runs through his writings and which, together with other of his positions, earned him suspicions of heresy.

personas/pedro-alvares-cabral/resumen.texto: Commander of the second Portuguese fleet to India, which in April 1500 touched the south coast of present-day Bahia and took possession of the land for Manuel I. He continued the voyage to Calicut and returned to Lisbon in 1501.

personas/pero-vaz-de-caminha/resumen.texto: Scribe of Cabral’s fleet; his letter to King Manuel I, dated May 1, 1500, is the first written description of the land and of the Tupiniquins. He died in December 1500 in the attack on the Portuguese trading post in Calicut.

personas/manuel-i-de-portugal/resumen.texto: King of Portugal (1495–1521) during the voyages of Vasco da Gama and Cabral. He received Caminha’s letter and in 1502 leased the brazilwood trade to a consortium headed by Fernão de Noronha.

personas/juan-iii-de-portugal/nacimiento.texto: Castle of São Jorge in Lisbon

personas/juan-iii-de-portugal/resumen.texto: King of Portugal (1521–1557). He divided the Brazilian coast into hereditary captaincies (1534–1536), created the general government (1548) and the bishopric of Bahia (1551), sent the first Jesuits, and established the Portuguese Inquisition (1536).

personas/sebastian-i-de-portugal/resumen.texto: King of Portugal from 1557. His law of 1570 prohibited enslaving the Indians of Brazil except those taken in an authorized just war and those who attacked Portuguese or other Indians in order to eat them. He died in the Battle of Alcácer Quibir, in Morocco, and his disappearance led to the union with Spain (1580).

personas/martim-afonso-de-sousa/resumen.texto: Leader of the 1530–1533 expedition that patrolled the coast against the French and founded São Vicente (1532), the first Portuguese town in Brazil. He received the captaincy of São Vicente and later served as governor of India (1542–1545).

personas/joao-ramalho/resumen.texto: Portuguese man who lived among the Tupiniquins of Piratininga before 1532, married according to Indigenous custom to Bartira, daughter of Tibiriçá. He served as an intermediary for Martim Afonso de Sousa and founded the town of Santo André; the Jesuits accused him of living in concubinage and of enslaving Indians.

personas/caramuru/resumen.texto: Portuguese castaway who from the early 16th century lived among the Tupinambá of the Bay of All Saints, married to Paraguaçu, and served as an intermediary for the donatary captains and Tomé de Sousa. His story became a founding legend in the poem Caramuru by Santa Rita Durão (1781).

personas/duarte-coelho/resumen.texto: Donatary captain of the Pernambuco captaincy (1534) and founder of Olinda (1535). His captaincy was one of the few that prospered, with sugar mills, wars against the Caetés and alliances with the Tabajaras.

personas/tibirica/resumen.texto: Leading Tupiniquim of Piratininga, father-in-law of João Ramalho, ally of the Portuguese and protector of the Jesuit college of São Paulo. Baptized as Martim Afonso, he defended the town against an attack by other Tupi in 1562 and died that same year.

personas/cunhambebe/resumen.texto: Leading Tupinambá of the Ubatuba region, ally of the French against the Portuguese and their Tupiniquim allies. Hans Staden, who was his prisoner, describes him as a warrior who boasted of having eaten many enemies; according to Thevet, he died in an epidemic around 1555.

personas/arariboia/resumen.texto: Leading Temiminó, ally of the Portuguese in the war against the Tamoios and the French of Guanabara (1567). Baptized as Martim Afonso, he received lands opposite Rio de Janeiro, where the village of São Lourenço, origin of Niterói, was formed.

personas/tome-de-sousa/resumen.texto: First governor-general of Brazil (1549–1553). He founded Salvador with about a thousand men, among them the first Jesuits, under royal instructions to punish hostile peoples and protect allies.

personas/pero-fernandes-sardinha/resumen.texto: First bishop of Brazil, based in Salvador, in conflict with the Jesuits and with Governor Duarte da Costa. On his return to Portugal he was shipwrecked on the coast of present-day Alagoas and, according to the chronicles, was killed and eaten by the Caetés (1556); his death served in 1562 to declare a just war against them.

personas/mem-de-sa/resumen.texto: Third governor-general (1558–1572). With Jesuit support he concentrated Indians in aldeias, waged war on the Tupinambá of the Paraguaçu and on the Caetés, destroyed the fort of Antarctic France in 1560 and consolidated Rio de Janeiro (1567).

personas/estacio-de-sa/resumen.texto: Nephew of Mem de Sá; he founded São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro on March 1, 1565. He died from an arrow wound received in the attack on the Tamoio villages of Uruçumirim (1567).

personas/villegaignon/resumen.texto: Knight of Malta and vice admiral of Brittany, who founded Antarctic France in Guanabara Bay (1555). His theological disputes with the Calvinists who had come from Geneva ended with their expulsion and the execution of three of them (1558).

personas/antonio-raposo-tavares/nacimien.texto: Freguesia de São Miguel do Pinheiro

personas/antonio-raposo-tavares/resumen.texto: Bandeirante born in Portugal who led the attacks on the Jesuit reducciones of Guairá (1628–1629) and of Tape (1636), and between 1648 and 1651 traveled about ten thousand kilometers down the Amazon. The Jesuits accused him of enslaving thousands of Guaraní; São Paulo historiography of the 20th century celebrated him as an expander of the territory.

personas/manuel-preto/resumen.texto: São Paulo bandeirante who led expeditions to capture Indians in Guairá from the early 17th century and, together with Raposo Tavares, the great attack on the reducciones of 1628–1629.

personas/fernao-dias/resumen.texto: São Paulo bandeirante who hunted Indians in the south in his youth and from 1674 led the expedition in search of emeralds in the interior of Minas, in which he had his mestizo son José Dias hanged for conspiring. He died of fever in the sertão; the region he crossed later became the gold region.

personas/domingos-jorge-velho/resumen.texto: Bandeirante hired by the government of Pernambuco for the Barbarian War and then against Palmares, which he took in 1694 with troops made up mostly of Indians. In a letter of 1697 the bishop of Pernambuco described him as one of the greatest “savages” he had known, who barely spoke Portuguese.

personas/salvador-de-sa/nombre.texto: Salvador Correia de Sá e Benevides

personas/salvador-de-sa/resumen.texto: Governor of Rio de Janeiro. With an armed fleet from Rio he recovered Luanda and Angola from the Dutch (1648), which restored the route of African slaves to Brazil.

personas/manuel-da-nobrega/resumen.texto: Head of the first Jesuits, who arrived with Tomé de Sousa in 1549, and first provincial of Brazil. He organized the aldeias, founded with Anchieta the Piratininga college (1554) and negotiated the Iperoig truce (1563); in a letter of 1558 he argued that conversion required first subjecting the Indians by force.

personas/jose-de-anchieta/resumen.texto: Jesuit born in Tenerife, who arrived in Brazil in 1553, co-founder of São Paulo (1554) and hostage of the Tamoios at Iperoig (1563). He wrote the first grammar of Tupi (1595), letters, plays in three languages and the poem De gestis Mendi de Saa; he was canonized in 2014.

personas/fernao-cardim/resumen.texto: Portuguese Jesuit who arrived in 1583 as secretary to the visitor Cristóvão de Gouveia, later rector of the Bahia college and provincial. His treatises on the land and people of Brazil, seized by English privateers in 1601, were first published in English without his name (1625).

personas/pero-de-magalhaes-gandavo/resum.texto: Portuguese humanist and copyist, author of the Tratado da terra do Brasil (c. 1570) and of the História da Província Santa Cruz (1576), the first printed history of Brazil. He is the source of the remark that the language of the coast had no F, L or R because its speakers had “neither faith, law, nor king.”

personas/gabriel-soares-de-sousa/resumen.texto: Sugar mill owner in Bahia who, in Madrid (1587), wrote the Tratado descritivo do Brasil to ask Philip II for permission and favors to search for mines. He died in 1591 on the mining expedition into the interior.

personas/andre-thevet/resumen.texto: Franciscan friar and later royal cosmographer who spent about ten weeks in Antarctic France (1555–1556). His Singularitez (1557) includes descriptions and engravings of the Tupinambá and of tobacco; Léry accused him of inventing what he claimed to have seen.

personas/jean-de-lery/resumen.texto: French Calvinist sent from Geneva to Antarctic France (1557); after the break with Villegaignon he lived for several months among the Tupinambá before returning to France. He was a pastor, survived the siege of Sancerre (1573) and published his History of a Voyage to the Land of Brazil in 1578.

personas/hans-staden/resumen.texto: Gunner from Hesse in the service of the Portuguese at the fort of Bertioga, captured by the Tupinambá in 1554; he lived about nine months as a prisoner in the Ubatuba region until a French ship rescued him. His True History (1557) is one of the most cited accounts of ritual anthropophagy.

personas/vicente-do-salvador/resumen.texto: Franciscan born in Bahia, author of the first history of Brazil written by someone born in the colony (1627). He was taken prisoner by the Dutch in the capture of Salvador (1624).

personas/claude-d-abbeville/resumen.texto: Capuchin of Equinoctial France; his History of the Mission (1614) describes the Tupinambá of Maranhão and the visit of six of them to Paris in 1613, where three died and the others were baptized, with King Louis XIII as godfather.

personas/antonio-vieira/resumen.texto: Jesuit born in Lisbon and raised in Bahia, preacher and diplomat of John IV. As superior of the Maranhão missions (1653–1661) he attacked the illegal enslavement of Indians in his sermons and obtained the law of 1655; the colonists expelled him along with the other Jesuits in 1661. He accepted African slavery and proposed bringing slaves from Angola, and the Inquisition prosecuted him (1663–1667) for his prophetic writings.

personas/andre-joao-antonil/resumen.texto: Jesuit born in Lucca, rector of the Bahia college, who under a pseudonym published Cultura e opulência do Brasil (1711), the most detailed description of the colonial economy; the crown ordered the edition recalled.

personas/francisco-de-orellana/resumen.texto: Captain from Extremadura, lieutenant of Gonzalo Pizarro on the expedition to the Land of Cinnamon (1541). Separated from the main group, he went down the Napo and the Amazon to the Atlantic with about sixty men (1541–1542); he returned as adelantado of New Andalusia and died in the Amazon delta in 1546.

personas/gaspar-de-carvajal/resumen.texto: Dominican friar who accompanied Orellana, lost an eye to an arrow and wrote the account of the descent of the river. He later continued his career in Peru and died in Lima.

personas/pedro-teixeira/resumen.texto: Portuguese captain who took part in the founding of Belém and in the expulsion of the English and Dutch from the Amazon, and who went up the river from Belém to Quito (1637–1638) and returned with Cristóbal de Acuña (1639).

personas/cristobal-de-acuna/resumen.texto: Jesuit from Burgos sent from Quito with Pedro Teixeira to describe the river (1639); his New Discovery of the Great River of the Amazons (1641) reports densely populated riverbanks.

personas/ajuricaba/resumen.texto: Leader of the Manao of the Rio Negro, a trading ally of the Dutch of the Essequibo, who resisted the Portuguese rescue troops. Captured around 1728, he died in transit to Belém: according to the Portuguese account, he threw himself into the river while in chains.

personas/charles-marie-de-la-condamine/r.texto: Mathematician of the French geodesic expedition to Quito (1735–1744). In 1743 he went down the Amazon to Pará, measuring its course, and in 1745 he published the first scientific description of the river, with information on rubber and curare.

personas/francisco-xavier-de-mendonca-fu.texto: Brother of Pombal and governor of the State of Grão-Pará and Maranhão (1751–1759). He applied the laws of 1755 freeing the Indians and drafted the Diretório dos Índios (1757), which took the aldeias away from the missionaries.

personas/alexandre-rodrigues-ferreira/re.texto: Naturalist from Bahia trained in Coimbra, who led the “philosophical voyage” through Grão-Pará, the Rio Negro and Mato Grosso (1783–1792), with artists who recorded Indigenous peoples, fauna and fortresses.

personas/mauricio-de-nassau/resumen.texto: Governor of Dutch Brazil for the Dutch West India Company (1637–1644). He built Mauritsstad, brought in painters and naturalists, tolerated Catholic and Jewish worship, and ordered the seizure of Elmina (1637) and Luanda (1641) to supply African slaves to the sugar mills.

personas/caspar-barlaeus/resumen.texto: Humanist from Amsterdam, who at Nassau’s commission wrote the official chronicle of his government in Brazil (1647).

personas/albert-eckhout/resumen.texto: Dutch painter in Nassau’s entourage. His full-length portraits of Tupi, Tarairiú, Africans and mestizos (1641) are among the first paintings of American peoples made from life; the “Tapuia woman” holds a severed human hand, an allusion to the funerary anthropophagy that the Dutch attributed to the Tarairiú.

personas/georg-marcgrave/resumen.texto: German naturalist and astronomer of Dutch Brazil, who set up an observatory in Recife and described hundreds of plants and animals for the Historia naturalis Brasiliae (1648). He died in Angola.

personas/willem-piso/resumen.texto: Physician to Nassau who described the diseases of Brazil and Indigenous remedies such as ipecac in the Historia naturalis Brasiliae (1648).

personas/filipe-camarao/resumen.texto: Leading Potiguara ally of the Portuguese and commander of Indigenous troops against the Dutch from 1630; he received the habit of the Order of Christ. In 1645 he exchanged letters in Tupi with his relative Pedro Poti, who fought on the Dutch side, and died after the first battle of the Guararapes.

personas/henrique-dias/resumen.texto: Commander of a regiment of Black soldiers, both free and enslaved, in the war against the Dutch (1633–1654); he fought at the Guararapes and received honors from the crown.

personas/ganga-zumba/resumen.texto: Leader of Palmares, called “king” in Portuguese documents, who in 1678 accepted an agreement with the government of Pernambuco: freedom for those born in Palmares and lands at Cucaú in exchange for submission. He died shortly afterward, according to some versions poisoned by opponents of the agreement.

personas/zumbi-dos-palmares/resumen.texto: Last leader of Palmares: he rejected the 1678 agreement and continued the war until the fall of Macaco (1694); he was killed in an ambush on November 20, 1695, and his head was displayed in Recife. His early biography (born in Palmares, raised by a priest) comes from the historian Décio Freitas, who cited letters that no other researcher has been able to locate.

personas/marques-de-pombal/nombre.texto: Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo, Marquis of Pombal

personas/marques-de-pombal/resumen.texto: Chief minister of Joseph I (1750–1777). In Brazil he promoted the laws freeing the Indians (1755) and the Diretório dos Índios, the monopolistic trading companies that brought African slaves to the Amazon and to Pernambuco, the expulsion of the Jesuits (1759) and the transfer of the capital to Rio (1763).

personas/tiradentes/resumen.texto: Ensign of the Minas cavalry and practical dentist; the only conspirator of the Inconfidência Mineira to be executed, hanged in Rio de Janeiro on April 21, 1792, and quartered. The Republic made him a national hero.

personas/jose-bonifacio/nombre.texto: José Bonifácio de Andrada e Silva

personas/jose-bonifacio/resumen.texto: Mineralogist trained in Coimbra and minister of Pedro I at independence. In 1823 he wrote for the Constituent Assembly a plan to attract the “wild” Indians by peaceful means, and a petition for the end of the slave trade and the gradual abolition of slavery.

personas/varnhagen/resumen.texto: Diplomat and historian, author of the História geral do Brasil (1854–1857) and discoverer and editor of the treatise of Gabriel Soares de Sousa. He defended war against and forced guardianship of the “wild” Indians, which set him against Indianist writers such as Gonçalves Dias.

personas/capistrano-de-abreu/resumen.texto: Historian from Ceará who edited Vicente do Salvador and Cardim, and who in Chapters of Colonial History (1907) shifted the focus from the coast to the settlement of the interior through cattle, the bandeiras and the roads.

personas/alfred-metraux/resumen.texto: Swiss ethnologist who in The Religion of the Tupinamba (1928) systematized what the chronicles say about the religion, shamanism, prophetic migrations and anthropophagy of the Tupi.

personas/gilberto-freyre/resumen.texto: Sociologist from Pernambuco, author of The Masters and the Slaves (1933), which presented Portuguese colonization as mixed and adaptable. His work was the basis of the idea of “racial democracy” and of the “lusotropicalism” adopted by Salazar’s regime; his critics pointed out that it minimizes the violence of slavery.

personas/florestan-fernandes/resumen.texto: Sociologist at the University of São Paulo who reconstructed Tupinambá society from the 16th-century chronicles and explained its war and anthropophagy as ritual revenge (1952). He later studied the integration of Black people into class society and criticized the idea of racial democracy.

personas/betty-meggers/resumen.texto: Smithsonian archaeologist who argued (1971) that the poor soils of Amazonia prevented large and complex societies, and that Marajoara was a culture that arrived from outside and declined. Later archaeology refuted those theses, although her ceramic chronology is still in use.

personas/anna-roosevelt/resumen.texto: American archaeologist whose excavations on Marajó (1991) and in the Santarém and Monte Alegre region argued that Amazonia had populous, complex societies and a human presence of about eleven thousand years.

personas/charles-boxer/resumen.texto: British historian of the Portuguese and Dutch empires, author of The Dutch in Brazil (1957) and The Golden Age of Brazil (1962). In Race Relations in the Portuguese Colonial Empire (1963) he discussed Freyre’s thesis of a Portuguese world without racism.

personas/stuart-schwartz/resumen.texto: American historian who, using the archives of sugar mills in Bahia, reconstructed the shift from Indigenous to African labor and the life of the enslaved (1985).

personas/john-hemming/resumen.texto: British historian and explorer, author of Red Gold (1978) and of its sequels on the history of the Indians of Brazil up to the 20th century.

personas/john-monteiro/resumen.texto: Historian at the University of Campinas; Negros da terra (1994) showed, using São Paulo inventories, that the economy of São Paulo in the 17th century depended on the labor of Indians captured by the bandeiras.

personas/boris-fausto/resumen.texto: Historian at the University of São Paulo, author of a História do Brasil (1994), which is the standard reference textbook of Brazilian history.

personas/juan-ii-de-portugal/resumen.texto: King of Portugal (1481–1495). He rejected the bull Inter caetera, which divided the lands found by Columbus, and negotiated with the Catholic Monarchs the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494), which set the line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands and left the eastern part of what would become Brazil on the Portuguese side.

personas/enrique-i-de-portugal/resumen.texto: Cardinal and inquisitor, regent for his great-nephew Sebastian and king from Sebastian's death at Alcácer Quibir (1578). Celibate, he failed to get the pope to release him from his vows, and he died on 31 January 1580 without naming a successor, with the kingdom in the hands of a council of five governors; his death opened the succession crisis that led to the union of Portugal, with its Brazilian empire, under the crown of Philip II.

personas/antonio-prior-de-crato/resumen.texto: Illegitimate grandson of Manuel I, acclaimed king in Santarém in July 1580 and defeated by the Duke of Alba at Alcántara (25 August); he resisted in the Azores until 1583 and afterwards lived in France and England. To win support against Philip II he offered concessions over Brazil: according to some versions, its cession to Catherine de' Medici, and in 1589 facilities in Brazil and the Azores for Elizabeth I.

personas/juan-iv-de-portugal/resumen.texto: Duke of Braganza, proclaimed king on 1 December 1640 (formally acclaimed on the 15th) when Portuguese independence was restored. His reign includes the creation of the General Company of Trade of Brazil (1649), which Vieira had proposed in 1643 on the Dutch model, and the expulsion of the Dutch from northeastern Brazil, completed in 1654.

personas/alfonso-vi-de-portugal/resumen.texto: He succeeded John IV at thirteen, with his mother as regent until 1662. During his reign, by the Treaty of The Hague (1661) the Netherlands recognized Portuguese sovereignty over Dutch Brazil, and by the Treaty of Lisbon (1668) Spain recognized the House of Braganza; his brother Pedro took over the government in 1667, was regent from 1668, and Afonso remained confined until his death.

personas/pedro-ii-de-portugal/resumen.texto: Regent from 1668 and king from 1683. His Brazilian policy sought metals and precious stones and to push the frontier as far as the Río de la Plata; during his reign gold was discovered in Minas Gerais, the Casa da Moeda mint was created (1694) and the quilombo of Palmares fell (1694–1695), and at the end of his life the dispute over Colonia del Sacramento, occupied by Spain in 1705, and the first clashes between paulistas and emboabas broke out.

personas/juan-v-de-portugal/resumen.texto: King of Portugal (1706–1750). Brazilian gold and diamonds, whose extraction was organized through the royal fifth and carried out mainly by African slaves, financed his policy and the convent-palace of Mafra; under the Treaties of Utrecht, France recognized Portuguese sovereignty between the Amazon and the Oiapoque in 1713, and Spain returned Colonia del Sacramento to Portugal in 1715; the Treaty of Madrid (13 January 1750) abandoned Tordesillas as the basis for the boundaries with Brazil.

personas/jose-i-de-portugal/resumen.texto: King of Portugal (1750–1777), who left the government in the hands of Pombal. During his reign the Treaty of Madrid (1750) was annulled by the Treaty of El Pardo (1761) after the Guarani War, the Jesuits were expelled from Brazil (1759), and the colony's capital was moved to Rio de Janeiro (1763).

personas/maria-i-de-portugal/resumen.texto: Queen of Portugal (1777–1816). By the Treaty of San Ildefonso (1777) Portugal ceded Colonia del Sacramento to Spain; a royal decree of 1785 banned almost all manufacturing in Brazil; by her decision, after the Inconfidência Mineira, most of those condemned to death were exiled and only Tiradentes was executed (1792). Declared incapable that year, she was governed in her name by her son John, and she died in Rio de Janeiro, where the court had departed in November 1807 and arrived in 1808.

personas/maria-quiteria/resumen.texto: Native of Bahia who enlisted disguised as a man, around September or October 1822, in the volunteer battalion of the Prince («Periquitos») of the Brazilian army besieging Salvador; General Labatut promoted her to cadet, and Pedro I gave her the Order of the Southern Cross in August 1823. Her year of birth is uncertain: 1792 according to a petition by her father in 1802, 1797 according to her death record.

hechos/pueblos-tupi-de-la-costa/titulo.texto: The Tupi peoples of the coast: Tupinambá, Tupiniquim, Potiguara and others

hechos/pueblos-tupi-de-la-costa/resumen.texto: Around 1500, Tupi-Guaraní-speaking peoples occupied almost the entire coast, from the Amazon to São Vicente (farther south were the Guaraní, called Carijó), having pushed peoples of other languages inland, whom they called “tapuias.” They lived in villages of large communal houses, grew manioc by slash and burn, fished and hunted, and were divided into groups hostile to one another (Tupinambá against Tupiniquim, Potiguara against Tabajara) that waged war to take captives. They formed no states: each village had its leaders and shamans, and the alliances were shifting, which the Portuguese and the French exploited.

hechos/antropofagia-tupinamba/resumen.texto: Authors from opposing camps—the Lutheran Staden, who was a prisoner, the Calvinist Léry, the Franciscan Thevet, and the Jesuits Nóbrega, Anchieta and Cardim—describe the same ritual: the war captive lived for months in the village of his captors, sometimes married to a woman of the group, until he was killed with a blow of a club at a public festival; then the whole village, women and children included, ate his flesh, and the killer took a new name. Florestan Fernandes (1952) explained it as ritual revenge that united the living with their dead. William Arens (1979) argued that American cannibalism was a European invention, but specialists on Brazil such as Donald Forsyth (1983 and 1985) answered him that the sources are independent and agree, including the Jesuit ones, which had no interest in inventing it. The crown used anthropophagy as a legal cause for enslavement (law of 1570).

hechos/pueblos-tapuia/titulo.texto: The “tapuias”: Ye and other peoples of the interior

hechos/pueblos-tapuia/resumen.texto: “Tapuia” was the name the Tupi gave to peoples of other languages, and the Portuguese used it for all the Indians of the sertão: Ye-speaking peoples (Aimoré or Botocudo, Kaingang, Kayapó, Timbira, Xavante, Akroá), Cariri, Tarairiú and others. Chroniclers described them as nomadic and unconquerable; the Aimoré halted the colonization of Ilhéus and Porto Seguro in the 16th century, and the Tarairiú of Janduí were allies of the Dutch. Their wars with the cattle ranchers of the Northeast (the Barbarian War) and with settlers in Minas and Espírito Santo (1808) were among the longest of the colony.

hechos/migraciones-profeticas-tupi/resum.texto: The chroniclers describe the karaí, prophets who traveled from village to village announcing a land without death or labor and who moved entire peoples to seek it. According to Spanish documents gathered by Métraux, several thousand Tupinambá left the Brazilian coast around 1539, and about three hundred survivors reached Chachapoyas, in Peru, in 1549, where their news of rich peoples downriver encouraged new expeditions to the Amazon. The interpretation of these movements as a search for the “Land without Evil” (Nimuendajú, Métraux, Hélène Clastres) is disputed by those who point to the weight of missionary translations in that idea (Judith Shapiro, 1987) or who see in the migrations also flights from the conquest.

hechos/santidade-de-jaguaripe/resumen.texto: A religious movement of Indigenous people in the Recôncavo of Bahia, led by a Tupi prophet named Antônio, who had passed through a Jesuit aldeia and mixed Tupi rites with Catholic figures (a “pope,” a “mother of God”), announcing the end of Portuguese rule. A sugar mill owner, Fernão Cabral de Taíde, protected it to attract labor, and the governor destroyed it in 1585. The Inquisition visit of 1591–1592 prosecuted the colonists who had tolerated it.

hechos/guerra-de-los-manaos/titulo.texto: The Manao War on the Rio Negro

hechos/guerra-de-los-manaos/resumen.texto: Portuguese rescue troops sailing up the Rio Negro clashed with the Manao of Ajuricaba, who traded with the Dutch of the Essequibo and, according to the Portuguese, sold them captives from other peoples. The government of Belém declared a just war; Ajuricaba was captured and died in transit, and many Manao and their neighbors were killed or enslaved. In the 20th century Ajuricaba became a regional symbol of Indigenous resistance.

hechos/cultura-marajoara/resumen.texto: A society of Marajó Island, at the mouth of the Amazon, which between c. 400 and 1400 built artificial earthen mounds (tesos) several meters high to live on and to bury its dead in large polychrome ceramic urns. Meggers and Evans interpreted it as a culture that arrived from northwestern South America and declined because of the poverty of the environment; Roosevelt (1991) and Denise Schaan showed that it was a long-lasting local development, with hierarchies and large populations sustained by fishing and agriculture.

hechos/cultura-santarem/resumen.texto: At the confluence of the Tapajós and the Amazon a populous society developed that produced very elaborate pottery (caryatid and spouted vessels) and extensive dark soils. Acuña (1641) and other 17th-century travelers describe them as a populous and feared people; the rescue troops and the Jesuit mission decimated them, and as a people they disappeared in the 18th century.

hechos/terra-preta/titulo.texto: Terra preta: the dark soils of Amazonia

hechos/terra-preta/resumen.texto: Dark, fertile soils formed by the accumulation of charcoal, pottery, bones and refuse in Indigenous settlements, found in patches of up to hundreds of hectares along Amazonian rivers. Most formed in the two millennia before the conquest and attest to long-lasting, populous settlements; today they are studied as a model of sustainable agriculture.

hechos/geoglifos-del-acre/resumen.texto: Hundreds of geometric ditched enclosures (circles, squares and combined figures up to 300 meters across), linked by roads, which deforestation has exposed since the 1970s in Acre and neighboring regions of Bolivia. Dates show that they were built and used for more than a millennium before the European arrival; the scarcity of domestic remains inside them supports the interpretation by Pärssinen, Schaan and Ranzi (2009) as ceremonial enclosures of a regional society.

hechos/aldeas-del-alto-xingu/titulo.texto: Fortified villages of the upper Xingu

hechos/aldeas-del-alto-xingu/resumen.texto: The ancestors of the peoples of the upper Xingu, such as the Kuikuro, lived between c. 1250 and 1650 in large villages with circular plazas, surrounded by ditches and palisades and linked by straight roads several kilometers long, with intensive management of the forest and wetlands. Heckenberger’s excavations with the Kuikuro suggest tens of thousands of inhabitants in the region, who declined in the 17th century, probably due to epidemics that arrived before the Europeans.

hechos/cultura-casarabe/titulo.texto: Casarabe culture of the Llanos de Mojos

hechos/cultura-casarabe/resumen.texto: A society of the flood-prone savanna of the Llanos de Mojos (Beni, Bolivia) which between c. 500 and 1400 built platforms, earthen pyramids, raised causeways, canals, dams and raised fields. The LiDAR survey published by Prümers et al. (2022) showed centers such as Cotoca and Landívar linked by causeways, a low-density urbanism; the Jesuit missionaries of Mojos (from 1682) found peoples of other origin there.

hechos/senorios-del-amazonas/resumen.texto: Carvajal (1542) describes along the Amazon lords with many subject peoples, such as Aparia and Machiparo, with continuous villages several leagues long, roads, food stores and fine pottery; Acuña (1641) confirms very populous riverbanks, especially that of the Omagua. By the end of the 17th century these populations were greatly reduced by epidemics, Portuguese rescue troops and transfers to the missions, and the surviving Omagua ended up in the missions of the Jesuit Samuel Fritz.

hechos/leyenda-de-las-amazonas/resumen.texto: Carvajal wrote that on June 24, 1542, the Spaniards fought against warlike women, tall and white, who commanded the Indians, and that a prisoner told them of a kingdom of women without men; hence the name of the river. Acuña gathered similar accounts, and La Condamine (1745) thought such a society might have existed. There is no archaeological evidence or independent document of a people of women; historians see in the account the projection of the Greek myth onto misunderstood Indigenous reports, perhaps of women who fought alongside the men.

hechos/debate-de-la-amazonia-pristina/re.texto: Meggers (1971) argued that the Amazonian environment prevented large societies and that the forest was nearly virgin. Denevan, who in 1976 estimated about 6.8 million inhabitants for greater Amazonia, and Roosevelt, Heckenberger, Neves and others responded with terra preta, mounds, geoglyphs and fortified villages, arguing that the population of 1492 was large and had transformed the forest. Critics of the stronger version (Crystal McMichael and others, with soil cores, in 2012 and 2017) accept the complex societies of the riverbanks, but maintain that much of the forest far from the rivers had little human intervention.

hechos/sambaquis/titulo.texto: The sambaquis: monumental shell mounds of the coast

hechos/sambaquis/resumen.texto: Mounds of shells, fish bones, earth and hearth remains raised by fishing, shellfish-gathering and foraging peoples along the Brazilian Atlantic coast, mainly from Santa Catarina to Rio de Janeiro, between about 8,000 and 1,000 years ago; the largest, near Laguna, exceed twenty meters in height. Many were used as cemeteries, with hundreds of burials, and in them appeared polished stone sculptures in the shape of animals (zoolites). Since the colonial period they were quarried to make lime, and the Brazilian law of archaeological monuments of 1961 expressly protects them.

hechos/llegada-de-cabral/resumen.texto: On April 22, 1500, the fleet of Pedro Álvares Cabral, bound for India, sighted Monte Pascoal and anchored off the south coast of present-day Bahia; it took possession of the “Land of Vera Cruz” for Manuel I, had peaceful contacts with the Tupiniquins, and continued the voyage on May 2, leaving two degredados behind. Whether the diversion was accidental or intended is debated (the thesis of an intentional discovery was held, among others, by Jaime Cortesão): no document proves prior knowledge. Months earlier, at the beginning of 1500, the Castilian Vicente Yáñez Pinzón had touched the northern coast of Brazil.

hechos/ciclo-del-palo-brasil/titulo.texto: The brazilwood trade and the trading posts

hechos/ciclo-del-palo-brasil/resumen.texto: In 1502 the crown leased the brazilwood trade, a red-dye tree that gave the land its name, to a consortium of Lisbon merchants led by Fernão de Noronha. Indians cut and loaded the logs in exchange for metal tools and other goods, at trading posts such as the one at Cabo Frio (1504). The French, above all Normans, competed in the same barter with the alliance of the Tupinambá, and the Portuguese responded with coastal patrol fleets in the 1510s and 1520s.

hechos/fundacion-de-sao-vicente/titulo.texto: Martim Afonso de Sousa founds São Vicente

hechos/fundacion-de-sao-vicente/resumen.texto: The expedition of Martim Afonso de Sousa (1530–1533), sent to expel the French and begin colonization, founded on January 22, 1532, the town of São Vicente, the first in Brazil, with its municipal council, and set up the first sugar mills in the region. It relied on the mediation of João Ramalho and of the Tupiniquins of Tibiriçá.

hechos/capitanias-hereditarias/resumen.texto: Between 1534 and 1536 John III divided the coast into strips that he granted as hereditary captaincies to twelve donatary captains, with powers of government, justice and land distribution, and with licenses to capture Indians and sell a certain number of them as slaves, even in Portugal. Only Pernambuco and São Vicente prospered; others failed for lack of resources and because of war with the Indians, such as Bahia, Ilhéus and Espírito Santo, which led to the creation of the general government (1549).

hechos/fundacion-de-la-santa-casa-de-san.texto: Founding of the Santa Casa de Misericórdia of Santos
Santa Casa de Misericórdia of Santos

Brás Cubas founded in 1543, in the port of Santos, a hospital with the Misericórdia brotherhood, considered the first in Brazil. It became the model for the Santas Casas that followed in Salvador, Olinda, Espírito Santo, Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, which cared for the sick, the poor, prisoners and orphans and were the main welfare network of colonial Brazil.

hechos/gobierno-general-del-brasil/titul.texto: Creation of the general government and founding of Salvador

hechos/gobierno-general-del-brasil/resum.texto: Tomé de Sousa arrived at the Bay of All Saints on March 29, 1549, with about a thousand men—soldiers, craftsmen, degredados and six Jesuits led by Nóbrega—and founded the city of Salvador, the capital of Brazil until 1763. Through Caramuru’s mediation, the Tupinambá of the bay worked on the construction in exchange for tools.

hechos/jesuitas-y-aldeias/titulo.texto: The Jesuits and the aldeias of Brazil

hechos/jesuitas-y-aldeias/resumen.texto: From 1549 the Jesuits gathered Indians of several groups into aldeias near the towns, with a church, a children’s school and crops, under a missionary who prohibited anthropophagy, polygamy and drinking festivals; in the 1560s there were tens of thousands of Indians in aldeias in Bahia, according to the Jesuits. The aldeias protected against direct enslavement, but they were also reserves of labor for settlers and the government and of allied warriors, and they concentrated people in the face of epidemics. The Jesuits composed grammars, catechisms and theater in Tupi and founded the colleges of Bahia, Rio, Olinda and São Paulo, the main education in the colony until 1759.

hechos/fundacion-de-sao-paulo/titulo.texto: Founding of the College of São Paulo de Piratininga

hechos/fundacion-de-sao-paulo/resumen.texto: On January 25, 1554, Jesuits sent by Nóbrega, among them Anchieta, celebrated Mass in the college built on the Piratininga plateau, next to the villages of Tibiriçá, where they taught Latin to the brothers and doctrine to the Indians. In 1560 the settlement merged with João Ramalho’s town of Santo André, and in the 17th century it was the base of the bandeiras.

hechos/francia-antartica/resumen.texto: A colony founded by Villegaignon in November 1555 on an island in Guanabara Bay, with the support of Admiral Coligny and in alliance with the Tupinambá (Tamoios). Calvinists who came from Geneva in 1557 clashed with Villegaignon, who expelled most of them and executed three. Mem de Sá’s fleet destroyed Fort Coligny in 1560, and the French who remained with the Tamoios were defeated in 1567.

hechos/guerra-de-los-tamoios/lugar.texto: Coast from Bertioga to Cabo Frio

hechos/guerra-de-los-tamoios/resumen.texto: An alliance of Tupinambá villages (Tamoios) on the coast between Bertioga and Cabo Frio, supported by the French, against the Portuguese of São Vicente and their Tupiniquim and Temiminó allies, whom they accused of raids to take slaves. After the Iperoig truce (1563) the war continued in Guanabara until the Portuguese victory of 1567; in the 1570s Governor Antônio Salema destroyed the last groups of Cabo Frio, killing and enslaving many according to the chronicles.

hechos/tregua-de-iperoig/resumen.texto: In 1563 Nóbrega and Anchieta went to Iperoig (Ubatuba) to negotiate with the Tamoios; Anchieta remained as a hostage for about five months while the agreement was concluded. The truce separated part of the Tamoios from the French for a time; according to Jesuit tradition, Anchieta composed there his poem to the Virgin, writing it in the sand.

hechos/campanas-de-mem-de-sa/titulo.texto: Mem de Sá’s campaigns against the Tupinambá and the Caetés

hechos/campanas-de-mem-de-sa/resumen.texto: Governor Mem de Sá imposed submission on the villages of Bahia: he prohibited anthropophagy, punished the villages that practiced it, and in 1559 burned numerous villages on the Paraguaçu River. In 1562 he declared a just war on the Caetés for the death of Bishop Sardinha, which made it lawful to enslave them; colonists also used it against Indians of the aldeias. Anchieta celebrated these campaigns in verse, and Nóbrega defended them as a condition for conversion.

hechos/epidemias-de-1562-1563/resumen.texto: Two epidemics, in 1562 and in 1563 (the latter smallpox), killed, according to Jesuit letters, a large part of the Indians of the Bahia aldeias; contemporary figures speak of about thirty thousand deaths. In the famine that followed, many Indians sold themselves or their children into slavery in exchange for food, and others fled into the interior. It is one of the best-documented episodes in the fall of the coastal Tupi population.

hechos/leyes-sobre-la-libertad-de-los-in.texto: Portuguese laws on the freedom of the Indians

The crown legislated again and again: the 1570 law prohibited enslaving Indians except in a just war or for anthropophagy; the 1595 law reserved to the king the declaration of a just war; the 1609 law declared all of them free, but the 1611 law again allowed captivity in response to colonists’ protests; Vieira obtained the 1655 law, and another, of 1680, prohibited it again and was revoked in 1688. Meanwhile “rescues” (purchase of captives from other Indians, presented as a way to save them from being eaten) and just wars continued, until the laws of 1755. Historians see in this oscillation the compromise between the pressure of the missionaries and that of the colonists, who needed labor.

hechos/esclavitud-indigena-en-brasil/tit.texto: Enslavement and forced labor of Indians

hechos/esclavitud-indigena-en-brasil/res.texto: Until the late 16th century the labor on the sugar mills of Bahia and Pernambuco was mostly Indigenous: captives of war, “rescued” Indians and aldeia workers paid with goods. Between 1570 and 1620 Africans replaced them on the sugar mills, due to epidemics, flights, the freedom laws and the masters’ preference; Schwartz and Monteiro discuss the weight of each cause. Indigenous slavery remained central in São Paulo, with the bandeiras’ “administrados,” and in Amazonia, with the rescue troops, until 1755.

hechos/ingenios-de-azucar/titulo.texto: The sugar mills of the Northeast

hechos/ingenios-de-azucar/resumen.texto: From the 1530s, and especially from 1570, Pernambuco and Bahia became the largest sugar producers in the world, on mills with dozens or hundreds of slaves, first Indians and then Africans. Antonil (1711) describes the continuous harvest, day and night, the punishments and the hierarchy of masters, cane farmers, free technicians and slaves; the religious orders, such as the Jesuits with the Sergipe do Conde mill, also owned mills and slaves.

hechos/trata-de-esclavos-hacia-brasil/ti.texto: The African slave trade to Brazil

hechos/trata-de-esclavos-hacia-brasil/re.texto: Brazil was the largest destination of the Atlantic slave trade: according to the Slave Voyages database (Eltis and Richardson), about 4.8 million Africans arrived, more than 40% of all those taken to the Americas, mainly from Angola and the Congo, from the Costa da Mina and, in the 19th century, from Mozambique. Merchants in Rio and Bahia controlled much of the traffic with Luanda and Ouidah, paid for with tobacco, liquor and gold. A law of 1831 prohibited it under British pressure, but it continued as contraband until the Eusébio de Queirós Law (1850).

hechos/union-iberica/titulo.texto: Union of the crowns of Portugal and Spain

hechos/union-iberica/resumen.texto: From 1580 to 1640 the kings of Spain, from Philip II onward, were also kings of Portugal, which kept its laws and administration. In Brazil the Tordesillas line lost force: the bandeirantes attacked the reductions of Guairá and Tape, and the Portuguese advanced along the Amazon. The enemies of Spain, above all the Netherlands, attacked Bahia (1624) and Pernambuco (1630); Portugal recovered its own king in 1640.

hechos/toma-de-salvador-1624/resumen.texto: The Dutch West India Company took Salvador in May 1624 and lost it in April 1625 to the “Jornada de los Vasallos,” a Spanish-Portuguese fleet under Fadrique de Toledo. Friar Vicente do Salvador lived through the occupation as a prisoner and recounted it in his history.

hechos/brasil-holandes/resumen.texto: The Dutch West India Company took Olinda and Recife in 1630 and came to dominate the coast from Sergipe to Maranhão. Under Nassau (1637–1644) Recife was urbanized, there was tolerance for Catholics and Jews—with the first synagogue in the Americas—and scientific and artistic activity unmatched in the colony, while the Company took Elmina and Luanda to supply slaves to the sugar mills. After the insurrection of 1645 and the defeats at the Guararapes, the Dutch capitulated in 1654 and renounced Brazil by the Treaty of The Hague (1661) in exchange for an indemnity.
