hechos/matanzas-de-cunhau-y-uruacu/resum.texto: At the start of the insurrection against the Dutch, Company troops with Tarairiú warriors led by the chief Janduí and allied Potiguara, guided by the German agent Jacob Rabe, killed the Catholic settlers gathered in the chapel of the Cunhaú mill during Mass (July 16, 1645), and others at Uruaçu (October 3). In 2017 the Catholic Church canonized thirty of those killed as martyrs.

hechos/insurreccion-pernambucana/resumen.texto: An uprising of Luso-Brazilian settlers, many of them in debt to the Company, led by João Fernandes Vieira and André Vidal de Negreiros, with troops of Indians led by Filipe Camarão and Black soldiers of Henrique Dias, against Dutch rule. The Brazilian national tradition saw in that alliance of “three races” the origin of the nation and of the Army; historians such as Boxer and Evaldo Cabral de Mello stress the interests of the sugar mill owners and the covert support of the Portuguese crown.

hechos/batallas-de-los-guararapes/resume.texto: Two battles in the Guararapes hills, south of Recife (April 19, 1648 and February 19, 1649), in which Luso-Brazilian, Indigenous and Black forces, which were outnumbered, defeated the Dutch. They were decisive for the Dutch capitulation of 1654; April 19 is Army Day in Brazil.

hechos/francia-equinoccial/titulo.texto: Equinoctial France and the conquest of Maranhão

hechos/francia-equinoccial/resumen.texto: In 1612 Daniel de La Touche, lord of La Ravardière, founded with Capuchins and the alliance of the Tupinambá the fort of Saint-Louis on the island of Maranhão. The Portuguese, with allied Indians, defeated the French at Guaxenduba (1614) and received the fort’s surrender in 1615; from there they advanced to the Amazon, and in 1621 the State of Maranhão was created, separate from Brazil.

hechos/fundacion-de-belem/resumen.texto: Francisco Caldeira Castelo Branco founded the fort of Presépio on Guajará Bay on January 12, 1616, the origin of Belém. The city was the base for the conquest of the Amazon: from it set out the troops that expelled the English and Dutch from the riverbanks and the rescue troops that captured Indians for the colonists.

hechos/expedicion-de-orellana/resumen.texto: Sent by Gonzalo Pizarro to look for food downriver during the expedition to the Land of Cinnamon, Orellana did not return; from late 1541 to the river’s mouth (August 1542) he went down the Napo and the Amazon with about sixty men, to reach Cubagua in September. It was the first European crossing of the river; Gonzalo Pizarro accused him of treason, and Carvajal’s account defends him.

hechos/expedicion-de-pedro-teixeira/resu.texto: With dozens of canoes, about seventy Portuguese soldiers and more than a thousand Indian oarsmen and archers, Teixeira went up from Pará to Quito (1637–1638) and returned with the Jesuit Acuña (1639). On the return he left a deed of possession for Portugal at the confluence of the Aguarico and the Napo, which the Portuguese invoked in the boundary negotiations of the 18th century.

hechos/tropas-de-rescate/resumen.texto: Official expeditions that went up the Amazon and its tributaries to “rescue” captives whom other Indians held in order to eat or sell them, and who could thus be legally enslaved; according to Vieira and other missionaries, and according to historians such as Hemming, they were often simple slave hunts. Together with the “descimentos” (transfer of entire peoples to the aldeias) and epidemics, they depopulated the banks of the Amazon and the Rio Negro until the mid-18th century.

hechos/revuelta-de-beckman/resumen.texto: In 1684 settlers of São Luís led by Manuel Beckman rose against the monopoly of the Maranhão Trading Company, which did not bring the African slaves it had promised, and against the Jesuits, who restricted the enslavement of Indians: they expelled them and deposed the government. In 1685 a new governor arrived, Beckman was hanged and the Jesuits returned; in 1686 the Regimento das Missões reorganized the aldeias.

hechos/bandeiras/resumen.texto: Armed expeditions that left São Paulo, with a few Portuguese and mamelucos and many Indians, to capture Indians, search for mines or, later, fight Indians and quilombos under contract with the government. In the 1620s to 1640s they attacked the Jesuit reductions of Guairá, Tape and Itatín, and at the end of the 17th century they found the gold of Minas. São Paulo historiography of the 19th and 20th centuries made them heroes of territorial expansion; Monteiro (1994) and others stress their slaving character.

hechos/ataques-al-guaira-y-al-tape/titul.texto: Bandeirante attacks on the Guairá and Tape reducciones

hechos/ataques-al-guaira-y-al-tape/resum.texto: In 1628–1629 a large bandeira led by Raposo Tavares and Manuel Preto attacked the Jesuit reducciones of Guairá, in the west of present-day Paraná, and took thousands of Guaraní to São Paulo; Ruiz de Montoya and other Jesuits gave figures of tens of thousands of captives, which historians treat as partial estimates. Facing new attacks, the Jesuits evacuated Guairá (1631) and, after the attacks on Tape (1636–1638), obtained permission to arm the Guaraní, who defeated a bandeira at Mbororé (1641).

hechos/bandeira-de-raposo-tavares/titulo.texto: Raposo Tavares’s bandeira to the Amazon

hechos/bandeira-de-raposo-tavares/resume.texto: An expedition of about two hundred paulistas and more than a thousand Indians left São Paulo in 1648, attacked the Itatín reducciones, passed into the Madeira basin and went down the Amazon to Gurupá, near Belém (1651), on a journey of about ten thousand kilometers from which few returned. Its aims—captives, mines, or reconnaissance of the territory for the crown—are debated.

hechos/quilombo-de-palmares/resumen.texto: A group of communities (mocambos) of runaway slaves in the Serra da Barriga and the forests of the interior of Pernambuco and Alagoas, mentioned from the early 17th century and which grew during the Dutch war. Portuguese and Dutch sources describe it with a “king” (Ganga Zumba), fortified villages, crops and thousands of inhabitants, and mention captives taken in raids on the sugar mills; the period figures of twenty thousand or more people cannot be verified. It resisted numerous Dutch and Portuguese expeditions until troops of Domingos Jorge Velho took the Macaco stockade in 1694.

hechos/acuerdo-de-cucau/titulo.texto: Ganga Zumba’s agreement with the government of Pernambuco

hechos/acuerdo-de-cucau/resumen.texto: In 1678 envoys of Ganga Zumba presented themselves in Recife before the governor and accepted an agreement: freedom for those born in Palmares, lands at Cucaú and recognition as vassals of the crown, in exchange for handing over the fugitives who arrived later. Zumbi and other leaders rejected it; Ganga Zumba died shortly after, and Cucaú was destroyed around 1680.

hechos/caida-de-palmares/titulo.texto: Capture of Macaco and death of Zumbi

hechos/caida-de-palmares/resumen.texto: In February 1694, after a siege, the paulista troops of Domingos Jorge Velho and those of Pernambuco took the Macaco stockade, capital of Palmares: hundreds of its inhabitants died and hundreds more were captured and sold. Zumbi escaped, was betrayed by a companion who had been captured, and was killed in an ambush on November 20, 1695; his head was displayed in Recife. November 20 is Black Consciousness Day in Brazil, a national holiday under a 2023 law.

hechos/guerra-de-los-barbaros/resumen.texto: A series of wars between cattle-ranching settlers advancing into the sertão of Bahia, Rio Grande, Paraíba and Ceará and the Tarairiú, Cariri and other “tapuia” peoples. The crown hired paulista tercios, such as that of Domingos Jorge Velho, and declared a just war, with massacres and the enslavement of prisoners; the killing of hundreds of Paiacu in 1699 by the field master Morais Navarro was investigated by the authorities themselves. The survivors were gathered into aldeias and their lands passed to the cattle estates.

hechos/fiebre-del-oro-de-minas/resumen.texto: Paulistas found alluvial gold in the interior of Minas in the 1690s; within a few decades tens of thousands of Portuguese and African slaves had arrived. Until the mid-18th century Brazil was the largest gold producer in the world, and the crown collected the royal fifth; in Minas, towns such as Vila Rica, Mariana and São João del-Rei arose, with Baroque churches and brotherhoods of Black and mulatto people. Part of the gold ended up in England through trade, as contemporaries already noted.

hechos/guerra-de-los-emboabas/resumen.texto: Conflict over control of the mines between the paulistas, who had found the gold, and the outsiders arriving from Portugal and other captaincies, the “emboabas.” After the episode at Capão da Traição (1709), in which surrendered paulistas were killed, the crown created the captaincy of São Paulo and Minas do Ouro, and many paulistas moved on to Goiás and Mato Grosso.

hechos/imprenta-en-el-brasil-colonial/ti.texto: The printing press banned in colonial Brazil

hechos/imprenta-en-el-brasil-colonial/re.texto: Unlike Spanish America, which had printing from 1539 in Mexico and 1584 in Lima, the Portuguese crown did not allow printing presses in Brazil: no general prohibition law is known, but those that were set up were closed by royal order. In 1747 a royal order required the closing of the press that António Isidoro da Fonseca had opened in Rio de Janeiro, where he had printed some pamphlets with the permission of local authorities, and the return of the type to Lisbon; earlier, in 1706, another in Pernambuco had been ordered seized. The first legal press was the Impressão Régia, created in 1808 with the arrival of the court.

hechos/educacion-superior-en-el-brasil-c.texto: No universities: higher education in colonial Brazil

Portugal created no universities in Brazil, while Spanish America had more than twenty before 1800: the sons of the elite studied at Coimbra, and the teaching of Latin, philosophy and theology was in the hands of the Jesuit colleges until their expulsion (1759). The first secular higher education was the Royal Academy of Artillery, Fortification and Design of Rio de Janeiro (1792), followed by the schools of surgery of Bahia and Rio (1808) and the Royal Military Academy (1810); the first permanent university was created in Rio de Janeiro in 1920.

hechos/compania-del-grao-para-y-maranhao.texto: General Company of Grão-Pará and Maranhão

A monopoly company created by Pombal in 1755, the same year as the laws freeing the Indians, to trade with the Amazon and bring African slaves to replace Indigenous labor; it transported thousands of Africans to Pará and Maranhão until its dissolution in 1778. It was followed by the Pernambuco and Paraíba Company (1759).

hechos/directorio-pombalino/resumen.texto: Applying the Diretório of 1757, the missionary aldeias of Amazonia and then of all Brazil became villages with Portuguese names, governed by lay directors, with compulsory Portuguese instead of the língua geral and mixed marriages encouraged. The Indians were free by law but obliged to work for the colonists and the state; the reports of the time record abuses by the directors, flights and the decline of the population of the villages. It was abolished by a carta regia of 1798.

hechos/expulsion-de-los-jesuitas-del-bra.texto: Expulsion of the Jesuits from Brazil

By law of September 3, 1759, Pombal expelled the Jesuits from Portugal and its dominions, accusing them of enriching themselves through trade, of resisting the Treaty of Madrid and of complicity in the attack on Joseph I (1758). In Brazil they were arrested and shipped out; their colleges, which were nearly all the secondary education of the colony, were closed, and their estates and sugar mills were confiscated and sold.

hechos/traslado-de-la-capital-a-rio/titu.texto: Transfer of the capital to Rio de Janeiro

hechos/traslado-de-la-capital-a-rio/resu.texto: The seat of the viceroy moved from Salvador to Rio de Janeiro, the port through which the gold of Minas left and the base of the disputes with Spain over the Colonia del Sacramento on the Río de la Plata.

hechos/descenso-del-amazonas-de-la-conda.texto: After completing the measurement of the meridian arc at Quito, La Condamine went down the Marañón and the Amazon from Jaén de Bracamoros to Pará (1743) and continued to Cayenne (1744), measuring latitudes, longitudes and the speed of the river. He drew the first scientific map of the Amazon and described rubber and curare.

hechos/viaje-filosofico/resumen.texto: Naturalist expedition of the Portuguese crown along the Amazon, the Rio Negro, the Madeira, the Guaporé and Mato Grosso, with the artists José Joaquim Freire and Joaquim José Codina; it gathered collections and memoirs on Indigenous peoples, agriculture and fortifications. Much of it remained unpublished until the 20th century, and the collections sent to Lisbon were taken to Paris by the French in 1808.

hechos/visitas-de-la-inquisicion-al-bras.texto: Brazil had no tribunal of its own: it depended on the Inquisition of Lisbon, which sent visitors to Bahia and Pernambuco (1591–1595), to Bahia (1618) and to Grão-Pará (1763–1769), and acted through commissioners and familiars. Its main defendants were New Christians accused of Judaizing, who were sent for trial in Lisbon, above all in the first half of the 18th century.

hechos/inconfidencia-minera/resumen.texto: A conspiracy of magistrates, priests, military officers and landowners of Vila Rica against the collection of back taxes (the “derrama”), inspired by the independence of the United States, to create a republic in Minas. It was denounced before it broke out (1789); after the trial, most of those convicted were exiled to Africa and Tiradentes was hanged in 1792.

hechos/conjuracion-bahiana/resumen.texto: A movement of tailors, soldiers and artisans, mostly free mulattos, with some slaves, who in August 1798 posted placards in Salvador calling for a republic, equality regardless of color and free trade. It was suppressed, and in 1799 four of its members were hanged and quartered.

hechos/traslado-de-la-corte-portuguesa/t.texto: Transfer of the Portuguese court to Brazil

hechos/traslado-de-la-corte-portuguesa/r.texto: Faced with the French invasion of Portugal, Prince Regent John, Queen Maria I and thousands of courtiers and officials embarked in November 1807 under British escort; they reached Bahia in January and Rio in March 1808. In Bahia he decreed the opening of the ports to friendly nations (January 28, 1808), ending the Portuguese commercial monopoly, and in Rio he created the Impressão Régia, the Banco do Brasil, the Botanical Garden and the Royal Library.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-escuela-de-cirugi.texto: Founding of the School of Surgery of Bahia

On February 18, 1808, during his stay in Salvador, Prince Regent John created a school of surgery at the Royal Military Hospital, housed in the former Jesuit college: it was the first medical school in Brazil. In November another was created in Rio de Janeiro.

hechos/guerra-a-los-botocudos/titulo.texto: War against the Botocudo and Kaingang

hechos/guerra-a-los-botocudos/resumen.texto: By carta regia of May 1808, the government of John VI organized military divisions in the Doce River valley, in Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo, against the Botocudo, whom it accused of killing settlers and of anthropophagy; in November it extended the war to the Kaingang of Guarapuava. Prisoners could be held as captives for ten years or more. Travelers such as Maximilian of Wied-Neuwied (1815–1817) described the violence of that frontier; the law of October 27, 1831 repealed the cartas regias.

hechos/reino-unido-de-portugal-brasil-y-.texto: United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves

On December 16, 1815, the Prince Regent raised Brazil to a kingdom united with Portugal, with Rio de Janeiro as the seat of the monarchy. John VI was acclaimed king in Rio in 1818 and returned to Lisbon in 1821 at the demand of the liberal revolution of Porto.

hechos/revolucion-pernambucana/resumen.texto: A republic proclaimed in Recife in March 1817 by merchants, priests, military officers and landowners, which lasted about two and a half months and spread to Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte. It kept slavery so as not to lose the support of the landowners; it was defeated by royal troops and several of its leaders were executed.

hechos/independencia-de-brasil/resumen.texto: After John VI’s return to Lisbon and the attempts of the Portuguese Cortes to reduce Brazil’s autonomy, Prince Regent Pedro refused to return (January 1822) and proclaimed independence on September 7, 1822, on the banks of the Ipiranga; he was acclaimed emperor in October and crowned in December. A war against the Portuguese troops followed in Bahia, Piauí, Maranhão, Pará and the Cisplatina until 1824, and Portugal recognized independence in 1825. The Empire kept slavery until 1888.

hechos/asedio-de-salvador-1822-1823/resu.texto: In the war of independence in Bahia, the Brazilian army formed in the Recôncavo, reinforced with troops from Pernambuco and Rio de Janeiro and commanded first by the French general Pierre Labatut, besieged Salvador, where Brigadier Madeira de Melo commanded the Portuguese troops loyal to the Cortes of Lisbon. The main clash was the battle of Pirajá (8 November 1822), and in May 1823 Thomas Cochrane's squadron arrived and blockaded the port. On 2 July 1823 Madeira de Melo evacuated the city with some 4,500 men in 83 vessels, although other accounts speak of a surrender; Bahia commemorates it as «2 de Julio».

hechos/restauracion-portuguesa-1640-1668.texto: After the coup of 1 December 1640 that brought the Duke of Braganza to the throne as John IV, Portugal and Spain fought a war of skirmishes and short campaigns on the border, with Portuguese victories at Montijo (1644), the Lines of Elvas (1659), Ameixial (1663) and Montes Claros (1665); the Treaty of Lisbon (1668) recognized the House of Braganza. Portugal sustained the effort with the wealth of its colonies, and in Brazil the 1641 truce with the Netherlands was not respected: the Dutch were expelled from the northeast in 1654 and recognized Portuguese sovereignty by the Treaty of The Hague (1661).

hechos/guerra-de-sucesion-portuguesa/res.texto: On the death without heir of the cardinal-king Henry (31 January 1580), Philip II of Spain and Antonio, prior of Crato, contested the crown. Antonio was acclaimed in Santarém in July, but the Duke of Alba defeated him at Alcántara on 25 August and took Lisbon; Antonio resisted in the Azores until the Santa Cruz fleet defeated his French allies at Ponta Delgada (July 1582), and Terceira fell in 1583. The Cortes of Tomar recognized Philip in 1581 on condition that the kingdom and its overseas territories, Brazil among them, keep their autonomy.

hechos/jornada-de-los-vasallos/titulo.texto: Jornada dos Vassalos: the reconquest of Salvador

hechos/jornada-de-los-vasallos/resumen.texto: Spanish-Portuguese fleet under Fadrique de Toledo, with the Portuguese part under Manuel de Meneses, which blockaded Salvador from late March 1625 and, with reinforcements from Pernambuco and São Vicente and the guerrillas who had been resisting in the Recôncavo, forced the Dutch to capitulate at the end of April; the sources give the fleet between 38 and 56 ships and between 12,000 and 14,000 men. Frei Vicente do Salvador, imprisoned during the occupation, recounted it in his history, and Spaniards and Portuguese disputed the credit in a «war of inks» that the Council of State halted by prohibiting the multiplication of accounts of the event.

lugares/salvador-de-bahia/resumen.texto: Founded by Tomé de Sousa in 1549 on the Bay of All Saints as the seat of the general government, it was the capital of Brazil until 1763, the seat of the first bishopric (1551) and of the main Jesuit college, and the great port of sugar and of the slave trade.

lugares/sao-paulo/resumen.texto: Born in 1554 as a Jesuit college on the Piratininga plateau, next to Tupiniquim villages. In the 17th century it was a poor, mestizo town where the língua geral was spoken, and the base of the bandeiras that captured Indians and searched for mines.

lugares/rio-de-janeiro/resumen.texto: Founded in 1565 by Estácio de Sá during the war against the French and the Tamoios in Guanabara Bay. It grew as the port of Minas gold, was the capital of the viceroyalty from 1763, seat of the Portuguese court (1808–1821) and capital of the Empire.

lugares/recife/resumen.texto: Port of Olinda, capital of Dutch Brazil (1630–1654), where Nassau built Mauritsstad and the first synagogue of the Americas operated. Afterward it became a center of the sugar trade and of the revolts of 1817 and 1824.

lugares/olinda/resumen.texto: Town founded by the donatary captain Duarte Coelho in 1535, seat of the Pernambuco captaincy, the richest in 16th-century Brazil thanks to its sugar mills. The Dutch burned it in 1631.

lugares/belem/resumen.texto: Born from the Presépio fort (1616), it was the base of the Portuguese conquest of the Amazon, of the rescue troops and of the missions, and the capital of the State of Grão-Pará and Maranhão.

lugares/sao-vicente/resumen.texto: First Portuguese town in Brazil, founded by Martim Afonso de Sousa in 1532, with the first sugar mills of the south.

lugares/sao-luis/resumen.texto: Founded by the French of Equinoctial France in 1612 and taken by the Portuguese in 1615; it was the capital of the State of Maranhão, the setting of Vieira’s sermons and of the Beckman revolt (1684).

lugares/porto-seguro/resumen.texto: Town and seat of the captaincy of the same name, on the coast where Cabral landed in 1500. Its captaincy was among those attacked by the Aimoré.

lugares/niteroi/resumen.texto: Born as the village of São Lourenço of Araribóia’s Temiminó Indians, allies of the Portuguese in the Guanabara war.

lugares/patio-do-colegio/resumen.texto: Site of the Jesuit college founded on January 25, 1554, in Piratininga, origin of the city of São Paulo; the current building is a 20th-century reconstruction.

lugares/santa-casa-de-santos/nombre.texto: Santa Casa de Misericórdia of Santos

lugares/santa-casa-de-santos/resumen.texto: Hospital founded by Brás Cubas in 1543 with the Misericórdia brotherhood, considered the first in Brazil and the model for the colony’s Santas Casas.

lugares/forte-do-presepio/resumen.texto: Wood-and-earth fort built in 1616 by Francisco Caldeira Castelo Branco on Guajará Bay, origin of Belém and of the Portuguese presence in the Amazon.

lugares/mauritsstad/resumen.texto: City planned by Nassau on Antônio Vaz Island, opposite Recife, with the Friburgo palace, gardens with plants and animals of Brazil, and an astronomical observatory, one of the first in the Americas.

lugares/isla-de-villegaignon/resumen.texto: Island in Guanabara Bay where Villegaignon built Fort Coligny in 1555, the center of Antarctic France, destroyed by Mem de Sá’s fleet in 1560; today it houses the Brazilian Naval School.

lugares/centro-historico-de-salvador/res.texto: Upper city of Brazil’s first capital, with the former Jesuit college, convents and churches of the 17th and 18th centuries. The neighborhood’s popular name, Pelourinho, comes from the pillory where enslaved people were publicly punished.

lugares/paco-imperial/resumen.texto: House of the governors of Rio de Janeiro, built in 1743, palace of the viceroys from 1763 and residence of Prince Regent John in 1808; the Portuguese empire was governed from there until 1821.

lugares/iglesia-de-san-francisco-de-ouro.texto: Church of Saint Francis of Assisi in Ouro Preto

Church of the Franciscan Third Order of Vila Rica, with design and sculptures by Antônio Francisco Lisboa, known as Aleijadinho, and paintings by Manuel da Costa Ataíde; it is a major work of Minas Baroque, financed by gold.

lugares/sinagoga-kahal-zur-israel/resume.texto: Synagogue of the Sephardic Jews of Recife during Dutch rule, considered the first in the Americas. After the capitulation of 1654 many of its members left for Amsterdam, the Caribbean and New Amsterdam.

lugares/serra-da-barriga/resumen.texto: Mountain range in present-day Alagoas where the Macaco stockade, capital of Palmares, was located and was taken in 1694; today it is the Quilombo dos Palmares Memorial Park.

lugares/ouro-preto/resumen.texto: Vila Rica, the center of gold mining in 18th-century Minas Gerais, with its Baroque churches and the scene of the Inconfidência Mineira (1789).

lugares/manaus/resumen.texto: It began as the fort of São José da Barra do Rio Negro (1669), the base of the rescue expeditions and of the Rio Negro missions.

lugares/kuhikugu/resumen.texto: One of the great pre-Columbian settlements of the upper Xingu, with ditches, plazas and roads, studied by Heckenberger with the Kuikuro.

lugares/biblioteca-nacional-de-brasil/re.texto: It grew out of the Royal Library brought from Lisbon by the court; it was created in Rio de Janeiro in 1810 and opened to the public in 1814. It is the largest library in Latin America.

lugares/jardin-botanico-de-rio/resumen.texto: Created by Prince Regent John in 1808 to acclimatize spices and useful plants brought from the East; it is one of the main scientific institutions in Brazil.

lugares/escuela-de-cirugia-de-bahia/resu.texto: The first medical school in Brazil, created in 1808 in the former Jesuit college in Salvador; it is the origin of the Faculty of Medicine of the Federal University of Bahia.

lugares/fortaleza-de-macapa/nombre.texto: Fortress of São José de Macapá

lugares/fortaleza-de-macapa/resumen.texto: Bastioned fortress built between 1764 and 1782 on the north bank of the Amazon's mouth to check the French of Guiana, using the forced labor of Indians from the Directorate villages and of African slaves, with high mortality and frequent escapes.

lugares/real-fuerte-principe-da-beira/re.texto: Fortress built from 1776 on the Guaporé River, across from the Spanish missions of Mojos, to secure the border fixed by the boundary treaties. It is one of the largest Portuguese fortifications in the interior of the Americas.
